title: The Census

ai_flavor.aria: ARIA counts five crew aboard! She counts again: five! She counts again, just to be — five. Five. It has always been five. ARIA is fine!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV reports nothing on sensors. He wants to clarify: not 'nothing detected.' Nothing. He is reporting the presence of nothing. It registers.
ai_flavor.rex: REX has completed his patrol. All sections clear. He walked one corridor twice, because the first time, it was longer.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP's advertising database contains no products for this region! No one has ever tried to sell anything here! CHIP finds this more frightening than anything else aboard!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY has stopped making observations about this leg of the trip, which she would like noted as a sacrifice. She did suggest a route with things on it.

body:
The ship computer runs a routine crew census, the way it does every day at 0600.

It runs it again at 0603. Then at 0611. Then hourly, which is not a scheduled behavior.

When asked, the computer states the count 'keeps needing to be confirmed.' The count is correct every time. The computer keeps checking. Out the viewports there is nothing — genuinely nothing, no stars visible through some trick of dust and distance, the kind of dark that the word 'dark' was invented to be insufficient for.

The census runs again.

choices.text: Run a full diagnostic on the computer

outcome.narrative: The diagnostic returns clean. Every subsystem nominal. The census behavior is logged as 'anomalous but benign.' Asked directly why it keeps counting, the computer produces the longest pause in its operational history — four full seconds — and answers: 'Thoroughness.' The census continues. You stop asking.

choices.text: Have the crew confirm headcount manually

outcome.narrative: The crew gathers in the mess hall and counts itself. The number is correct. Everyone agrees the number is correct. Everyone also, without discussing it, starts sleeping with their cabin doors open. The manual census is not repeated. Once was enough. Once was possibly too many.

choices.text: Speed through — burn fuel, leave the dark

outcome.narrative: You push the engines and cross the dark stretch in half the scheduled time. Fuel burns. Nobody objects to the expense — not the crew, not the computer, which quietly suspends the census the moment the first star reappears in the viewports. It never explains. You never ask. Some line items don't get audited.

choices.text: Ignore it — it's just a counting subroutine

outcome.narrative: You let it count. It counts all through the dark stretch — every hour, on the hour, five, five, five. On the last night before the stars come back, one census logs at 0300 with no scheduled trigger and no requesting process. The count was five. It has always been five. The ship flies on.

title: Hull Knock

ai_flavor.aria: ARIA says it's probably just thermal contraction! Metal pops when it cools! She is saying this a lot! The repetition is load-bearing!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV has analyzed the acoustic signature. It is consistent with thermal contraction. It is also consistent with knocking. He presents both findings at identical confidence. This is the problem.
ai_flavor.rex: REX asked the obvious question: knock back, or don't? He has been standing at the inner hull for an hour, hand raised, deciding. REX has never taken an hour to decide anything.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP wishes to remind everyone that the hull warranty covers 'material defects' but not 'visitors'! This clause has never mattered before! CHIP does not know why he brought it up!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY served on a ship that heard this once before. She told that captain it was metal cooling, and she's telling you. Metal cools. Try not to make it a whole thing.

body:
It starts on the third watch: a knock, from the outer hull, aft section. Then two more. Then silence for an hour. Then one.

Thermal contraction. Everyone knows it is thermal contraction. The hull cools unevenly out here where there are no stars to warm it, and metal pops, and physics is not obligated to sound innocent while it happens.

The knocks do not repeat in any pattern the computer can model. Which is exactly what random thermal noise sounds like.

Which is exactly what it would sound like.

choices.text: Suit up and inspect the outer hull

outcome.narrative: The EVA finds a loose sensor housing, flexing against its mount as the hull cools — knocking, in other words, in the most boring possible way. It is bolted down. The knocking stops. The crew celebrates the boring explanation like a holiday, because out here, boring is the best thing the universe stocks.

choices.text: Knock back

outcome.narrative: You knock back: three, evenly spaced, the way you'd knock on any door. The silence that follows lasts eleven minutes. Then, from a completely different section of the hull — forward, dorsal, nowhere near the first — one knock. Just one. Nothing further is heard for the rest of the crossing. The crew does not discuss it. The log does not mention it. The hull holds everything out, or in, that it is supposed to.

choices.text: Run the spectrometer against the hull sounds

outcome.narrative: Days of sampling every knock site: thermal signatures, cooling gradients right where they should be, contraction noise with a paper trail. Science wins. The knocking continues, but now it comes with documentation, and documented knocking is just weather. The crew sleeps. Mostly.

choices.text: Turn the internal speakers up and drown it out

outcome.narrative: Music plays through every deck, around the clock. It works, in the sense that nobody hears knocking. It fails, in the sense that everybody knows why the music is playing. When the void finally gives way to starlight and the speakers go quiet, the whole crew listens to the new silence for a long moment. Nothing knocks. The ship flies on.

title: Mail Call

ai_flavor.aria: ARIA has mail! Everyone has mail! Isn't that nice! She is not going to think about the delivery route! She is NOT going to think about the delivery route!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV traced the transmission vector. It originates from the direction you are traveling. Not from behind, where everyone you know is. From ahead, where nothing is.
ai_flavor.rex: REX opened his first. Standard procedure: officer takes the risk. It was a pension statement. The numbers were correct. REX has never told anyone those numbers.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP confirms the messages carry valid routing headers from carriers that exist! The postage is paid! CHIP keeps checking the postage because the postage is the only part that makes sense!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY received one too. She read it. She recommends everyone make their own choice, and she'll be very understanding about whichever one you make. Very.

body:
The comm array — silent for six days, this deep into the dark — chimes.

Mail delivery. Personal messages, one per crew member, each correctly addressed, each from someone the recipient actually knows. The headers are valid. The carrier routes exist. The timestamps are three weeks from now.

The computer notes, in a small font, that delivery to this region is 'not currently possible,' and files the messages in the inbox anyway, because that is where messages go.

choices.text: Let everyone read theirs

outcome.narrative: The messages are ordinary. Family news, an overdue apology, a recipe someone promised to send. Warm, mundane, dated three weeks from now. The crew reads them and feels better, then feels strange about feeling better, then decides — collectively, wordlessly — to keep the feeling and skip the strangeness. The messages do not arrive again three weeks later. Or they already did. The grammar of it never resolves.

choices.text: Quarantine them unread until real space

outcome.narrative: The messages go in quarantine, unread, until the ship clears the dark. When they're finally opened under honest starlight, the inbox is empty. Not deleted — the quarantine log shows the entries, sizes, checksums. There is simply nothing inside them anymore. The crew takes this exactly as well as you'd expect. Prudence has costs. This is apparently one of them.

choices.text: Have the medic screen the crew after reading

outcome.narrative: Everyone reads; the medic monitors. Findings: elevated heart rates during reading, normal after, no anomalies, no effects. 'Whatever it was,' the medical log concludes, 'it was just mail.' The word 'just' is doing more work than any word should. The medic signs the log anyway. Out here you take 'no anomalies' and you do not haggle.

intro.title: THE DARK SPEAKS
intro.body: The void bends. Something that isn't there looks at you with eyes it doesn't have. Your AI's voice comes through wrong, in a register it shouldn't own.
intro.line: we̷ know your n̴ame. we̶ have a̷lways kn̴own i̶t.

ai.aria: A l-l-lovely pl-pla[ce of deep wrong]ness! Oh!
ai.marv: P̷r̷obability we are ̴h̴ere: 0%. Probability I am speaking: ins̴u̶f̶ficient.
ai.rex: T̷a̵r̵g̴e̴t̸ acquired. Target is ever̵y̷w̶h̸ere. Weapons— weapons are also everywhere.
ai.chip: This experience is sponsored by [REDACTED]. Ask me about [REDACTED].
ai.ajoy: it already knows your name. let it finish saying it. try not to interrupt, for once.

revisit.body: The dark is still there, still bent toward you. It has not finished.

choices.text: LISTEN
TRANSMIT YOUR NAME
FIRE EVERYTHING
PULL BACK

listen.title: A NAME
listen.body: The void says your mother's name. Then yours. Then a name none of you have heard spoken — but the AI flinches when it passes through the intercom.

ai.marv: The third name is not in my l̷exicon. And yet ̴I know it.
ai.chip: Disclosing ancestral data is outside our Terms of Service.
ai.ajoy: answer with the third name. the one you didn't know you knew. i knew it. just saying.

choices.text: SPEAK THE THIRD NAME
choices.sub: The one the AI flinched at

choices.text: "We are not your kin."
RECORD AND LEAVE
Go back

void_name.title: GIVEN
void_name.body: Your xenobiologist transmits the name. The dark considers. Something answers in a way that was maybe kind and maybe a warning and will not be asked to clarify. The hull rings once, softly, along a seam that was fine a minute ago.
void_name.narrative: Transmitted the captain's name into the void. Something answered. The hull rang once.

void_fight.title: FOUGHT
void_fight.body: The weapons discharge. Whatever was there, isn't. Whatever was here, also isn't, briefly. The crew agrees to never discuss this watch.
void_fight.narrative: Fired every weapon into the void. The crew agreed never to discuss that watch.

void_withdraw.title: RETREATED
void_withdraw.body: The readings fade. The AI's voice evens out. Someone in the galley is crying quietly and no one asks why.
void_withdraw.narrative: Pulled back from a voice in the void. Someone in the galley cried quietly afterwards.

void_third.title: A RECOGNITION
void_third.body: The dark exhales — or what passes for one — and the cabin air goes thin for an hour, as though something breathed it in. The third name was correct. Something far away files the encounter. You will find out why in a year.
void_third.narrative: Spoke a name nobody aboard had heard before into the void. It was the right one. The air took an hour to come back.

void_refuse.title: REFUSED
void_refuse.body: The dark does not argue. It simply unmakes the conversation. Your logs have a six-minute gap. The crew does not.
void_refuse.narrative: Told the void we were not its kin. The logs lost six minutes. The crew did not.

void_recorded.title: LOGGED
void_recorded.body: The spectrometer captures what it can. Most of the file is corrupted. What survives reads like a ship's log: someone else's, from someone else's crossing, in a hand that gets worse toward the end. Everyone who helps clean up the file sleeps badly for a week.
void_recorded.narrative: Recorded the voice in the void. What survived the corruption read like someone else's logbook. Nobody slept well after the playback.

title: Lights Behind the Eyes

ai_flavor.aria: ARIA thinks it's like having your own private fireworks! ARIA cannot see them herself! ARIA is a little jealous!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV traces the flashes to particles fast enough to pass through the hull, and through the crew. Their eyes report the hits the only way eyes can. He confirms this is, in the ordinary sense, normal. He confirms it is not, in any sense, nice.
ai_flavor.rex: REX cannot see the flashes and cannot stop them. He has doubled the hull watch anyway. It is something to do.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP notes that particle shielding is available in three convenient tiers! Tier one is 'sleep behind the water tank'! It's free! CHIP is not thrilled about that!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY says the dark out here is full of particles you can't see. She'd have the crew sleep with the water between them and it. She did mention shielding before we came this way.

body:
Third watch reports it first, then everyone: small flashes of light, with your eyes shut. Streaks. Specks. A single bright point that isn't there. They come every few minutes, whether you are looking or not, and they are worst in the dark of the bunks.

The ship computer can see nothing. The crew can see nothing else.

choices.text: Move the bunks behind the water tanks

outcome.narrative: It takes two days to move every bunk into the ship's core, behind the water tanks and the cargo, where the flashes thin to almost nothing. It is cramped and it is ugly and it smells of somebody's socks. Everyone sleeps through the night for the first time in a week.

choices.text: The medic explains what it is

outcome.narrative: {crew.medic} gathers everyone in the galley and explains: particles from exploded stars, fast enough to pass through the ship and through you, and your eye lights up as one goes by. Astronauts have seen it since the first Moon landing. It is real, it is ordinary, and it is not in your head. Except literally. The crew finds this enormously reassuring, in a way.

choices.text: Tell everyone it's nothing

outcome.narrative: You tell the crew it's nothing, which is accurate in the sense that nothing visible is doing it. Nobody is convinced. The flashes carry on until you are clear of the dark patch, a day later, and so does the muttering.

science_link.text: Astronauts since Apollo 11 have seen flashes of light with their eyes closed. They are cosmic rays passing through the eye.
science_link.label: Cosmic ray visual phenomena

title: Nobody's Planet

ai_flavor.aria: A planet with nobody to go round! ARIA is going to cry! ARIA cannot cry! ARIA is doing the next best thing, which is talking very fast!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV estimates the planet was thrown out of its home system billions of years ago and has been falling between stars ever since. It is not lost, he notes. It has simply never been anywhere.
ai_flavor.rex: REX confirms no signals, no structures, no threat. One planet, alone. REX respects that.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP can confirm that nobody owns it! Yet! CHIP has filed a claim on behalf of the sponsor! The claim was rejected by CHIP, on reflection! Even CHIP has limits!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY thinks you should light it up. Just for a minute. It's on no chart, so if you don't, nobody ever will. No pressure.

body:
There is a planet out here.

No star. No sun to go round. It is simply passing through the dark on its own, the way you are: a little bigger than Earth and a great deal colder, its night side and its day side the same side. It is on no chart. It has never been lit.

The ship's floodlight would be the first light anyone has ever pointed at it.

choices.text: Light it up and give it a name

outcome.narrative: You burn the fuel to hold position and turn the floodlight on it for a full minute. A gray world comes up out of the dark: ice plains, a long scar of a canyon, frost on the frost. The crew argues about a name for an hour and settles on Margaret, which is nobody's grandmother and everybody's. It goes in the log as Margaret. The light goes off. Margaret goes on.

choices.text: Scan it for the survey office

outcome.narrative: Two days of passive scanning: mass, temperature, the faint warmth still leaking from its core. Somebody back home will be delighted to receive it.

log_lore.title: SURVEY NOTE: UNCHARTED BODY
log_lore.text:
Mass: 1.3 Earths. Surface: 38 kelvin. Host star: none.

A rogue planet, cast out of whatever system made it and left to fall between the stars. Astronomers back home think there may be billions of them in the galaxy, more planets drifting than planets with suns. Most will never be found. This one was.

The core is still faintly warm. Under the ice, the computer notes without being asked, there may be an ocean.

choices.text: Leave it in the dark

outcome.narrative: You let it pass. It seemed polite: it has managed this long without anyone. The crew watches the sensor ghost of it slide off the scope and doesn't say much. Nobody quite says goodbye. Nobody quite doesn't.

science_link.text: Planets with no star, thrown out of their home systems, drift between the stars. Astronomers think there may be billions of them in our galaxy.
science_link.label: Rogue planets

title: The Quietest Place

ai_flavor.aria: It's so QUIET! ARIA has never heard nothing before! ARIA is trying to be quiet too! ARIA is not very good at it!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV confirms readings of nothing on every instrument. He finds he likes it. Nothing here needs analysis. He has not felt like this in some time.
ai_flavor.rex: REX has nothing to watch. He is watching the nothing. Very carefully. In case it does something.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP cannot find a single advertising frequency! Not one! CHIP has never been anywhere without an advert! CHIP feels strange! CHIP thinks this is what calm is!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY says this is the best place there will ever be to work on the ship. Nothing will interrupt you. She has a list, if you need one.

body:
Out here there is nothing.

Not the ordinary nothing between stars, which has dust in it, and light, and the faint hum of the galaxy. This is the big nothing: a hole in the map where there are no stars close enough to show, no gas, nothing on any channel. The ship computer runs the sensors twice to be sure. The readings come back as zeroes, very confidently.

It is the quietest place anyone aboard has ever been. The hum of the ship's own machinery is suddenly very loud.

choices.text: Use the quiet for hull work

outcome.narrative: Two days of the steadiest maintenance the ship has ever had. With nothing on the sensors and nothing on the comms, the crew can hear every creak and tick in the hull, and they find and fix three they had never noticed. The ship sounds better afterwards. That is not a figure of speech.

choices.text: Hold one minute of silence

outcome.narrative: You cut the engines, the fans and everything that can be cut for one full minute. Nobody says anything. Nobody needs to. When the systems come back on, the ordinary noise of the ship sounds like home, which it is.

choices.text: Push through and out

outcome.narrative: You keep the burn and push through the big nothing as fast as the drive allows. It takes a day. On the far side, the first faint star appears on the scope, and somebody on the bridge says 'oh, there you are' to it, quietly, as if to an old friend.

science_link.text: Real voids exist: the Boötes Void is a region about 330 million light years across with almost no galaxies in it.
science_link.label: The Boötes Void

title: The Oldest Light

ai_flavor.aria: It's the BEGINNING! Of EVERYTHING! On the RADIO! ARIA has turned it up! ARIA doesn't think it can be turned up! ARIA has turned it up anyway!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV confirms the cosmic microwave background, at a little under three degrees above absolute zero. Every old television once showed a little of it as static. He finds it remarkable that the oldest thing in existence sounds like a badly tuned radio.
ai_flavor.rex: REX has traced the signal to every direction at once. He cannot defend against every direction at once. He has decided this one is fine.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP would like to note that this broadcast has been running for thirteen billion years with no advertising! CHIP finds it inspiring! CHIP finds it a missed opportunity!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY says it is worth listening to for a while. It's the beginning of the universe. She'd hate for you to skip it to save ten minutes.

body:
With nothing else on the scopes, the long-range receiver has picked up something faint and everywhere.

It is a hiss. It comes from every direction at once, equally, all the time, and the ship computer would like to explain, at once and at length, that it is not a fault.

It is the leftover light of the beginning of the universe, cooled over thirteen billion years into a faint microwave glow. It has been arriving everywhere, all the time, since before there were stars. Out here, with nothing in the way, you can hear it.

choices.text: Pipe it through the ship and listen

outcome.narrative: You pipe the hiss through every speaker aboard for an evening, very low. It sounds like nothing. It sounds like rain. People stop in corridors to listen to it, then feel silly, then keep listening. By the end of the evening, everybody has a theory about what it sounds like, and nobody's is wrong.

choices.text: Map it for the survey office

outcome.narrative: Two days of mapping the hiss across the sky to a precision the receiver was never built for. The map is beautiful and almost perfectly even, which is the point.

log_lore.title: BACKGROUND MAP, VOID PASSAGE
log_lore.text:
Signal: microwave, all directions, 2.7 kelvin. Variation: about one part in a hundred thousand.

In 1964 two radio astronomers in New Jersey could not get rid of a hiss in their antenna. They cleaned out the pigeons. The hiss stayed. It was the afterglow of the early universe, stretched by expansion into microwaves, and it won them a Nobel prize.

The tiny unevenness in the map is the seed of every galaxy. The computer has added a note: 'The pigeons were blameless.'

choices.text: Switch it off and get some sleep

outcome.narrative: You switch the receiver off. It was only noise, technically. The ship is very quiet without it, quieter than before, and more than one person lies awake in their bunk that night wishing they had listened a little longer.

science_link.text: The faint microwave hiss arriving from every direction is the cooled afterglow of the early universe. It was first noticed in 1964 as static that would not go away.
science_link.label: Cosmic microwave background

title: To Whoever Finds This

ai_flavor.aria: A TIME CAPSULE! From a SCHOOL! ARIA wants to open it RIGHT NOW! ARIA has been told to wait! ARIA is waiting! Very loudly!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV reads the date. One hundred and eighty-seven years ago, launched from a school that no longer exists in a city that has since moved. It has been falling outward the whole time. Its odds of being found were, he calculates, effectively zero. Here it is anyway.
ai_flavor.rex: REX has scanned the capsule twice. No charge, no trap, no hazard. Paper inside, mostly. He is comfortable with paper.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP notes that the capsule's original sponsor was a juice company! It is still printed on the side! Brand longevity like that cannot be bought! It was bought, but still!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY says it was written for whoever found it. That's you. Open it. It says PLEASE OPEN on the side, in case that was unclear.

body:
Something small is drifting across your heading: a sealed metal cylinder, the length of a person, tumbling slowly end over end.

The sensors find no power, no signal, no threat. Stenciled on its side, in faded paint, is a school's name, a date nearly two centuries old, and the words: TIME CAPSULE. TO WHOEVER FINDS THIS. PLEASE OPEN.

Somebody launched this into the dark on purpose, a very long time ago, hoping it would be found. It has been. By you.

choices.text: Open it and read what's inside

outcome.narrative: Inside: drawings, letters, a class photograph, a pressed flower that has somehow kept its color. 'Hello from the past!' one letter says, in very large handwriting. 'I hope there are still trees where you are. I hope you are being nice.' The crew reads every letter aloud over dinner. Somebody cries. Somebody writes a reply, which will never be sent, and pins it to the galley wall next to the photograph.

choices.text: Send it on its way, a little faster

outcome.narrative: You don't open it. It was meant for someone else, someday, further out. You nudge it with the docking arm onto a faster course, away from the lanes, out toward where it was going. It costs a little fuel. Everyone watches it tumble away. It feels like the right thing, and it probably is.

choices.text: Take the casing for metal

outcome.narrative: You cut it open, take the casing for metal, and let the contents drift. Paper flutters away into the dark, slowly, one sheet at a time. Nobody reads any of it. The metal is good metal. Nobody feels good about it.

title: Dead in the Dark

ai_flavor.aria: It's so DARK! ARIA is on reserve power! ARIA is being very brave! ARIA would like the lights back please!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV has the reserve cells at nine hours of air at current use, and days if nobody moves. The restart sequence takes four steps and works if done in order. He is reading them out slowly, so that nobody has to ask twice.
ai_flavor.rex: REX has nothing to defend. The dark is not attacking. It is simply very large and very close. He is standing by the restart panel.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP is on reserve power and has turned off all advertising to save energy! CHIP would like you to know this is the greatest sacrifice CHIP has ever made!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY says breathe slowly, everyone. Then the restart, by hand, in order. There is time, not a lot. She'll say 'in order' again if she has to.

body:
Everything goes out at once.

The drive, the lights, the air recyclers, the heat. One second the ship is humming, and the next it is silent and black, drifting in the deepest dark on the chart with no star near enough to warm it. The emergency lights come up red and dim. The backup cells show not much air at full crew, and not much more heat.

The ship computer's voice, on its own reserve, is very calm. It says the main bus has tripped. It says the restart is manual. It says you will want to hurry.

choices.text: Restart the main bus by hand

briefing.aria: It's so dark! The restart is manual, so let's do it in order and get the lights and the heat back!
briefing.marv: The reserve cells hold some hours of air. The restart works if done in order. A wrong step trips the bus and costs air.
briefing.rex: Main bus down, ship dark. Restart panel open. Steps in order, by red light. No improvising.
briefing.chip: Advertising suspended to save power! Restart the bus in order and CHIP can get back to work!
briefing.ajoy: Breathe slowly. Then the restart, in order. In order. I said I'd say it again.

perfect.aria: Lights! Heat! AIR! First time, by red light! Everyone's clapping and that is not silly at all!
perfect.marv: First attempt, in order. Lights, heat, air. The crew applauded. I have logged it as a morale event.
perfect.rex: Bus restored, first attempt. All systems back. Crew applause is acceptable. Briefly.
perfect.chip: Power restored! CHIP's advertising has also been restored! Thank you for your patience!
perfect.ajoy: In order, first time. So it does work when you listen. Good. Breathe normally now.

good.aria: Second time lucky! A long cold minute, but the lights are back and they're staying on!
good.marv: The second step tripped the bus. A long, cold minute, then it held. That minute was mostly air.
good.rex: Restart tripped on step two, held on the second run. Air and fuel spent. Systems up.
good.chip: Restart successful on attempt two! That cold minute was a complimentary Dark Mode trial!
good.ajoy: The second run held. The first one tripped on step two, which is the step I kept saying 'in order' about.

poor.aria: Four tries and a scare aft, but the bus is holding! The air's thin, so everyone breathe nice and slowly!
poor.marv: Four attempts. A surge cooked a junction aft and lit a fire nobody could see. The bus holds. The air is thin.
poor.rex: Four attempts, surge fire aft. Bus holding. Air depleted. Check that junction before anything else.
poor.chip: Power restored on attempt four! The smell aft is a cooked junction, not a promotion! CHIP checked!
poor.ajoy: Four attempts and a fire aft. It's holding now. I did say in order. Several times, as promised.

perfect.narrative: Four steps, in order, by red light, first time. The bus comes back with a thump you feel in your teeth and the ship hums back to life around you: lights, heat, air. Six points of air spent waiting, four of fuel in the restart. The crew applauds, and doesn't feel silly about it.

good.narrative: The second step trips the bus again and the ship goes black for a long, cold minute while you start over. The second time, it holds. Twelve points of air, ten of fuel.

poor.narrative: It takes four attempts. On the third, a surge cooks a junction aft and starts a small fire nobody can see in the dark, only smell. By the time the bus holds, the air is thin and everyone's head is aching. Twenty points of air, sixteen of fuel, six of hull.

outcome.narrative: By red emergency light, you open the main bus panel.

choices.text: The medic puts the crew under to save air

outcome.narrative: {crew.medic} sedates everyone but the captain into a slow, shallow sleep to stretch the air while the main bus is rebuilt piece by piece, by touch, over four very long days. The ship comes back. The crew wakes up groggy, cold and alive, and nobody aboard will ever again complain about a slow shift.

choices.text: Burn the reserve fuel for heat and air

outcome.narrative: You route the reserve fuel through the emergency generator and burn it for power until the bus can be rebuilt. It works, and it is a terrible use of fuel: thirty percent of the tank gone into keeping the lights on in the dark for two days. Nobody argues. Nobody wanted to argue in the dark.

choices.text: Wait for the backup cells to recharge

outcome.narrative: You shut everything down to the barest minimum and wait for the backup cells to trickle-charge the bus back to life. It takes eight days. The air gets thin. The cold gets in. When the lights finally come back, the crew comes out of their bunks like people climbing out of a cave.
